But it is rather the meadow-saffron: the Hebrew means radically a plant with a pungent bulb, inapplicable to the rose. So Syriac. It is of a white and violet color [Maurer, Gesenius, and Weiss]. In North Palestine, between Mount Tabor and Lake Tiberias (<reference osisRef="1Chr.5.16">1Ch 5:16</reference>). Septuagint and Vulgate translate it, "a plain"; though they err in this, the Hebrew Bible not elsewhere favoring it, yet the parallelism to valleys shows that, in the proper name Sharon, there is here a tacit reference to its meaning of lowliness. Beauty, delicacy, and lowliness, are to be in her, as they were in Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>). <div eID="gen12890" type="x-p"/>

Historically fulfilled in the joy of Simeon and Anna in the temple, over the infant Saviour (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.25-Luke.2.38">Lu 2:25-38</reference>), and that of Mary, too (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">Lu 1:53</reference>); typified (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.9-Exod.24.11">Ex 24:9-11</reference>). Spiritually, the bride or beloved is led (<reference osisRef="Song.2.4">So 2:4</reference>) first into the King's chambers, thence is drawn after Him in answer to her prayer; is next received on a grassy couch under a cedar kiosk; and at last in a "banqueting hall," such as, Josephus says, Solomon had in his palace, "wherein all the vessels were of gold" (Antiquities, 8:5,2). The transition is from holy retirement to public ordinances, church worship, and the Lord's Supper (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>). The bride, as the queen of Sheba, is given "all her desire" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.13">1Ki 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Ep 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16-Eph.3.21">16-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.19">Php 4:19</reference>); type of the heavenly feast hereafter (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Is 25:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen12898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his banner ... love--</hi>After having rescued us from the enemy, our victorious captain (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">He 2:10</reference>) seats us at the banquet under a banner inscribed with His name, "love" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>). His love conquered us to Himself; this banner rallies round us the forces of Omnipotence, as our protection; it marks to what country we belong, heaven, the abode of love, and in what we most glory, the cross of Jesus Christ, through which we triumph (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Ro 8:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.57">1Co 15:57</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>). Compare with "over me," "underneath are the everlasting arms" (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.27">De 33:27</reference>). <div eID="gen12899" type="x-p"/>

The "stay" she prayed for (<reference osisRef="Song.2.5">So 2:5</reference>) is granted (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">De 33:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.24">Psa 37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.16">Is 41:16</reference>). None can pluck from that embrace (<reference osisRef="John.10.28-John.10.30">Joh 10:28-30</reference>). His hand keeps us from falling (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.30">Mt 14:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.14.31">31</reference>); to it we may commit ourselves (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Psa 31:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left hand--</hi>the left is the inferior hand, by which the Lord less signally manifests His love, than by the right; the secret hand of ordinary providence, as distinguished from that of manifested grace (the "right"). They really go together, though sometimes they seem divided; here both are felt at once. Theodoret takes the left hand, equivalent to judgment and wrath; the right, equivalent to honor and love. The hand of justice no longer is lifted to smite, but is under the head of the believer to support (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">Is 42:21</reference>); the hand of Jesus Christ pierced by justice for our sin supports us. The charge not to disturb the beloved occurs thrice: but the sentiment here, "His left hand," &c., nowhere else fully; which accords with the intensity of joy (<reference osisRef="Song.2.5">So 2:5</reference>) found nowhere else; in <reference osisRef="Song.8.3">So 8:3</reference>, it is only conditional, "should embrace," not "doth." <div eID="gen12904" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8215"/><div sID="gen12905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8215"/><hi type="bold">7. by the roes--</hi>not an oath but a solemn charge, to act as cautiously as the hunter would with the wild roes, which are proverbially timorous; he must advance with breathless circumspection, if he is to take them; so he who would not lose Jesus Christ and His Spirit, which is easily grieved and withdrawn, must be tender of conscience and watchful (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">Eze 16:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.19">1Th 5:19</reference>). In Margin, title of <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Psa 22:1</reference>, Jesus Christ is called the "Hind of the morning," hunted to death by the dogs (compare <reference osisRef="Song.2.8">So 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>, where He is represented as bounding on the hills, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">Psa 18:33</reference>). Here He is resting, but with a repose easily broken (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zep 3:17</reference>). It is thought a gross rudeness in the East to awaken one sleeping, especially a person of rank.<div eID="gen12905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my love--</hi>in Hebrew, feminine for masculine, the abstract for concrete, Jesus Christ being the embodiment of love itself (<reference osisRef="Song.3.5">So 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.8.7">8:7</reference>), where, as here, the context requires it to be applied to Him, not her. She too is "love" (<reference osisRef="Song.7.6">So 7:6</reference>), for His love calls forth her love. Presumption in the convert is as grieving to the Spirit as despair. The lovingness and pleasantness of the hind and roe (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Pr 5:19</reference>) is included in this image of Jesus Christ.<div eID="gen12906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Canticle II.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.2.8-Song.3.5">So 2:8-3:5</reference>)--John the Baptist's Ministry. <div eID="gen12907" type="x-p"/>

Loving reassurance given by Jesus Christ to the bride, lest she should think that He had ceased to love her, on account of her unfaithfulness, which had occasioned His temporary withdrawal. He allures her to brighter than worldly joys (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mi 2:10</reference>). Not only does the saint wish to depart to be with Him, but He still more desires to have the saint with Him above (<reference osisRef="John.17.24">Joh 17:24</reference>). "The summoned bride is welcome," say some fathers, "to weave from them garlands of beauty, wherewith she may adorn herself to meet the King." Historically, the flowers, &c., only give promise; the fruit is not ripe yet; suitable to the preaching of John the Baptist, "The kingdom of heaven is at hand"; not yet fully come.<div eID="gen12916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the time of ... singing--</hi>the rejoicing at the advent of Jesus Christ. Gregory Nyssenus refers the voice of the turtledove to John the Baptist. It with the olive branch announced to Noah that "the rain was over and gone" (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">Ge 8:11</reference>). So John the Baptist, spiritually. Its plaintive "voice" answers to his preaching of repentance (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jr 8:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">7</reference>). Vulgate and Septuagint translate, "The time of pruning," namely, spring (<reference osisRef="John.15.2">Joh 15:2</reference>). The mention of the "turtle's" cooing better accords with our text. The turtledove is migratory (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jr 8:7</reference>), and "comes" early in May; emblem of love, and so of the Holy Ghost. Love, too, shall be the keynote of the "new song" hereafter (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Is 35:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.3">14:3</reference>; 19:6). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8222"/><div sID="gen12921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8222"/><hi type="bold">14. dove--</hi>here expressing endearment (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference>). Doves are noted for constant attachment; emblems, also, in their soft, plaintive note, of softened penitents (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">Is 59:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">Eze 7:16</reference>); other points of likeness are their beauty; "their wings covered with silver and gold" (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.13">Psa 68:13</reference>), typifying the change in the converted; the dove-like spirit, breathed into the saint by the Holy Ghost, whose emblem is the dove; the messages of peace from God to sinful men, as Noah's dove, with the olive branch (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">Ge 8:11</reference>), intimated that the flood of wrath was past; timidity, fleeing with fear from sin and self to the cleft Rock of Ages (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Is 26:4</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.11">Ho 11:11</reference>); gregarious, flocking together to the kingdom of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">Is 60:8</reference>); harmless simplicity (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>).<div eID="gen12921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clefts--</hi>the refuge of doves from storm and heat (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.28">Jr 48:28</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Jer.49.16">Jr 49:16</reference>). Gesenius translates the Hebrew from a different root, "the refuges." But see, for "clefts," <reference osisRef="Exod.33.18-Exod.33.23">Ex 33:18-23</reference>. It is only when we are in Christ Jesus that our "voice is sweet (in prayer, <reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">Mt 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Ga 4:6</reference>, because it is His voice in us; also in speaking of Him, Mal 3:16); and our countenance comely" (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">Ex 34:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">71:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Is 33:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen12922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stairs--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.20">Eze 38:20</reference>, Margin), a steep rock, broken into stairs or terraces. It is in "secret places" and rugged scenes that Jesus Christ woos the soul from the world to Himself (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mi 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.14">7:14</reference>). So Jacob amid the stones of Beth-el (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.11-Gen.28.19">Ge 28:11-19</reference>); Moses at Horeb (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.1-Exod.3.22">Ex 3:1-22</reference>); so Elijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.9-1Kgs.19.13">1Ki 19:9-13</reference>); Jesus Christ with the three disciples on a "high mountain apart," at the transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.1">Mt 17:1</reference>); John in Patmos (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.9">Re 1:9</reference>). "Of the eight beatitudes, five have an afflicted condition for their subject. As long as the waters are on the earth, we dwell in the ark; but when the land is dry, the dove itself will be tempted to wander" [Jeremy Taylor]. Jesus Christ does not invite her to leave the rock, but in it (Himself), yet in holy freedom to lay aside the timorous spirit, look up boldly as accepted in Him, pray, praise, and confess Him (in contrast to her shrinking from being looked at, <reference osisRef="Song.1.6">So 1:6</reference>), (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">He 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>); still, though trembling, the voice and countenance of the soul in Jesus Christ are pleasant to Him. The Church found no cleft in the Sinaitic legal rock, though good in itself, wherein to hide; but in Jesus Christ stricken by God for us, as the rock smitten by Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.20.11">Nu 20:11</reference>), there is a hiding-place (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Is 32:2</reference>). She praised His "voice" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.8">So 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>); it is thus that her voice also, though tremulous, is "sweet" to Him here. <div eID="gen12923" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 14. dove-- here expressing endearment ( Psa 74:19 ). She praised His "voice" ( So 2:8 , 10 ); it is thus that her voice also, though tremulous, is "sweet" to Him here.
